pages.x: On 23 October 1956 students marched through Budapest in support of reformers in Poland, demanding free elections and the withdrawal of Soviet troops. By evening a huge crowd had pulled down the giant statue of Stalin, leaving only his boots. At the radio station the secret police opened fire, and the protest became a revolution.

Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest the next morning. Young fighters, many of them teenagers, met them with rifles and petrol bombs from alleys and courtyards such as the Corvin Passage. On 25 October security forces fired on a peaceful crowd outside the Parliament, killing scores of people.

The party turned to Imre Nagy, a reforming communist it had thrown out the year before. At first he hesitated, then he came over to the revolution. He promised free elections, and on 1 November, as fresh Soviet troops poured into the country, he declared that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact and be neutral.

For a few days Hungary was free. The Soviet tanks pulled out of Budapest, political prisoners were released, and new parties and newspapers sprang up. Workers' councils ran the factories, and Cardinal Mindszenty, jailed for years, was set free.

In Moscow, Nikita Khrushchev wavered, then on 31 October decided to crush the revolution, while Britain and France, attacking Egypt over the Suez Canal, were in no position to protest. Hungary's radio stations sent desperate calls for help to the West. None came.

Before dawn on 4 November a massive Soviet force stormed Budapest. Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy, and a new government was announced under János Kádár. The fighters held out for a week in the working-class districts and factories, but the revolution was crushed.

About 2,500 Hungarians and 700 Soviet soldiers died. Some 200,000 Hungarians fled across the border to Austria, and the West took them in. Nagy was lured out of the embassy with a promise of safety, seized, and after a secret trial hanged in 1958.
pages.of: Hungarians who fled to the West

pages.x: Kádár ruled Hungary for 32 years. After years of reprisals, in which hundreds were executed, he loosened his grip in the 1960s, and allowed small freedoms and more food and goods in the shops. "Whoever is not against us is with us," he said. Hungarians called it goulash communism.

The revolution showed the world that Soviet rule in eastern Europe rested on tanks. In June 1989 a quarter of a million people came to Nagy's reburial in Budapest, and that October, on the anniversary of the rising, Hungary became a republic again. 23 October is now a national holiday.
pts: Crushed by Soviet tanks on 4 November
